<reflection>
The first experiment provided baseline kinetic data. The fitting results show that all candidate mechanisms except M20 have very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values (ranging from -22.76 to -22.29), indicating that they fit the data almost equally well. M20 has a significantly higher NLL (-11.71), making it implausible. The aim of the first turn was to obtain an initial profile, but it did not effectively discriminate among the remaining 19 mechanisms. Therefore, a new experiment is needed to stress key mechanistic differences.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the closely fitting mechanisms, we propose an experiment with added initial product. This tests two key features: (1) reversibility of the catalytic steps, which affects all mechanisms with reversible elementary reactions, and (2) product-induced deactivation, which is specific to mechanisms like M12 and M17. 

- For reversible mechanisms without product deactivation (e.g., M1, M2, M5, M6, M7, M8), added product will reduce the net forward rate due to thermodynamic reversibility, but the progress curve will still exhibit a smooth exponential approach to a lower equilibrium conversion. The catalyst remains fully active throughout.

- For mechanisms with product-induced deactivation (M12: P+cat=>inactive_catP; M17: P+catS=>inactive_catSP), added product will cause irreversible loss of active catalyst, leading to a faster decay of the reaction rate and a premature plateau in conversion. The final conversion will be lower than that predicted by reversible equilibrium alone.

- Other deactivation mechanisms (e.g., M9, M14) are not directly accelerated by product, so their behavior may resemble reversible mechanisms but with additional curvature from deactivation; however, the added product will not specifically enhance deactivation.

By comparing the progress curve with added product to the first run (no product), we can identify whether product merely shifts the equilibrium or also actively inactivates the catalyst. This experiment directly targets the mechanistic difference between reversible inhibition and irreversible deactivation, separating M12 and M17 from the rest of the top candidates.
</hypothesis>
